# Helping your midwife find you

## Because we would rather be beside you than driving past your house for the third time

**Riverside Community Midwives | Home Birth Welcome Pack**

When your baby is on the way, we want to get to you quickly, bring in our equipment and help you feel safe and supported.

What we do **not** want to do is spend twenty minutes looking for Flat 14, park half a mile away, or discover that your house has no number and a sat nav with a sense of humour.

A few simple preparations can make a big difference—especially at 3am, in the rain, when every street looks exactly the same.

You do not need a perfect house. You do not need to bake anything. We just need to find your door, get inside safely and reach you with all our bags.

## First things first: 37 weeks

**Home birth cover starts from 37 weeks of pregnancy.**

If labour starts **before 37 weeks, go to hospital**. Do not wait at home for the home birth team.

From 37 weeks, if you think labour is starting, telephone the **Riverside birth line**. Please do not wait until morning because you are worried about disturbing us. Night-time babies are rather fond of arriving at night, and we are used to it!

If you think you or your baby needs urgent medical help at any time, **call 999 straight away**. Then call the birth line if you can.

## Who to call when labour starts

**Call the Riverside birth line—not your own midwife’s personal mobile.**

Your named midwife may be off duty, asleep, on holiday or attempting to eat a hot meal. The birth line connects you with the midwife who is on call, so it is the quickest and safest way to reach the team.

Save the number in your phone and in your partner’s or support person’s phone. Keep it on the fridge too.

**Riverside birth line: ______________________________**

When you call, please tell us:

- Your **full name**.
- How many weeks pregnant you are, or your due date.
- That you are planned for a **Riverside home birth**.
- What is happening—for example, whether you are having contractions or your waters have broken.
- Your **full address and postcode**, including the flat number, floor and building name if you live in flats.
- The best telephone number for us to call you back on.
- Anything we need to know about getting in, such as a gate, entry phone or difficult-to-find entrance.
- Any parking restrictions outside your home.
- If you think the baby is coming quickly, tell us straight away.

Keep your phone nearby after calling. If your partner or support person made the call, please make sure their phone stays switched on and nearby too.

## Send us a location as well as an address

An address is useful. An exact location is even better.

You can send a **WhatsApp location pin to the birth line phone**. This lets us see where to go on a map.

You can also use **what3words**. The app gives three words for a small, exact location. Send us the three words for the door or entrance you want us to use—not simply the middle of a large building.

If technology is not your thing, do not worry. Clear directions are absolutely fine. Tell us useful details such as:

- “It is the blue door next to the corner shop.”
- “Our entrance is at the back of the building.”
- “Use the gate on Eaton Road, not the front entrance.”
- “The lift is broken, so please use the stairs.”

**Please do not post your address, entry code or location pin in the Facebook group.** Send these privately to the birth line.

### A small warning about flat numbers

One of our midwives once drove around a block of flats in Everton for twenty minutes looking for Flat 14. She found Flat 13 easily enough. Flat 14, however, was in a completely different building. Naturally.

In the end, dad appeared at a window waving a tea towel. It worked beautifully, but we would prefer to know your exact building before labour gets going!

## Help us recognise your house

Please make your house number or name as easy to see as possible. If it is missing, tiny or hidden behind a very enthusiastic bush, you could make a large temporary sign and put it somewhere visible from the road.

At night, switch on your **porch light or another outside light**. This is a huge help on dark winter evenings. A light also helps us avoid walking confidently up the wrong path.

Coloured balloons or something bright on the gate are another excellent idea. One family did this for us and we found them immediately. It does not have to be fancy. You are having a baby, not organising a royal garden party.

We once visited a house called **Rosemary Cottage**, which had no number and sat in the middle of a long row of terraces. The sat nav helpfully took us to a chip shop. Very nice chips, but not the right destination.

If your house has only a name, please explain exactly where it is—for example, “Rosemary Cottage, between numbers 24 and 28, opposite the red post box.”

## Leave the front door closed—we will knock

Please make sure someone can hear the doorbell, knocking or entry phone when we arrive. If it is safe, your partner or another adult can wait near the entrance or meet us outside when we say we are close.

The person in labour should stay comfortable and safe inside. There is no need for you to stand at the gate directing traffic while having contractions!

One of our midwives once walked through an open door into the wrong house. The very nice gentleman inside gave her a Jammie Dodger anyway. We appreciated the biscuit, but it would have been even better to find the right family first.

## Parking: two midwives, two cars, many bags

**Two midwives come for the birth, and we usually travel in separate cars.** If possible, please leave two parking spaces close to your home. If that is not possible, tell us where visitors can legally park nearby.

For the birth, we may be carrying:

- Entonox cylinders—the gas and air you may use for pain relief.
- Large equipment and emergency bags.
- Monitoring equipment.
- Birth pool equipment, if you are using a pool.
- Various other bags that seem to multiply in the boot.

The closer we can park, the quicker and easier it is to bring everything in. Our arms will already be full enough without an obstacle course.

If you live in a parking permit area, including parts of **Anfield and Kensington**, please ask your local council how visitor permits work. Have any visitor permits ready so we can put them on the dashboard. We have received parking tickets before, and they are much less exciting than babies.

If you cannot arrange permits or nearby parking, just tell us when you call. We would rather know in advance than discover it while circling the block.

## Clear the way inside

Please keep the **hallway, stairs and route to your birth room clear**.

Before we arrive, ask your partner or support person to move:

- Shoes and boots.
- Washing baskets.
- Bags and coats.
- Toys, especially Lego.
- Anything else we might trip over while carrying equipment.

We do not care about dust, washing-up or whether your sofa matches your curtains. We do need to get safely through the door and up the stairs without standing barefoot on Lego. Few things test a midwife’s professional calm quite like Lego in the dark.

If you are planning to use a birth pool, it also helps to clear the route to the room where it will be set up.

## Pets: we love them, but please give them their own room

Please arrange for dogs and other lively pets to stay safely in another room during the birth, with water and anything they need. Your partner or support person can check on them when possible.

We know they are part of your family. We also know they may be excited, worried or determined to investigate our bags.

One of our midwives is greatly loved by a Staffordshire bull terrier called **Pippin**. Pippin demonstrated his love by jumping up at every visit, and she nearly dropped the Entonox. He is a wonderful dog. He is not a wonderful equipment assistant.

During labour—and especially during pushing—we need space to move and work safely. Your pet can come back for introductions afterwards.

## Even if you have done this before, please help us again

If this is your second, third or fourth home birth, you may know exactly what to expect. However, you might have different midwives this time, or we may arrive in the dark.

Please still share your address, access details and parking information. We will not assume that your previous directions have been passed on perfectly. “It is easy when you know” is normally followed by someone getting lost.

---

# Fridge checklist: Helping your midwives find you

**Put this somewhere everyone can see. Your partner or support person can use it too.**

## Before 37 weeks

☐ Save the **Riverside birth line** in at least two phones.  
**Birth line: ______________________________**

☐ Write down your **full address, postcode, flat number and building name**, if needed.

☐ Prepare a **WhatsApp location pin or what3words address** for the correct entrance.

☐ Check your house name or number can be seen from the road.

☐ Check the porch or outside light works.

☐ Think about where **two midwives in separate cars** can park.

☐ If you live in a permit area, ask the council about **visitor permits**.

☐ Decide who will clear the hallway, put pets in another room and guide the midwives in.

☐ Remember: **if labour starts before 37 weeks, go to hospital.**

## When labour starts—from 37 weeks

☐ Call the **Riverside birth line**, not your midwife’s personal mobile.

☐ Give your name, full address, callback number and explain what is happening.

☐ Tell us about the entrance, access codes, flat number and parking restrictions.

☐ Send your location pin or what3words address **privately to the birth line phone**.

☐ Switch on the porch or outside light.

☐ Put out a clear house-number sign, bright marker or balloons if helpful.

☐ Have visitor parking permits ready for the dashboard.

☐ Clear shoes, washing baskets, toys and **Lego** from the hallway and stairs.

☐ Put pets safely in another room.

☐ Make sure someone can hear us knocking, ringing or calling.

☐ Keep the phone nearby and follow the on-call midwife’s advice.

☐ If you or your baby needs urgent help, **call 999 straight away**.

## A final welcome from us

In the Philippines, we think of the midwife as being like family. We love that idea. When we come through your door, we bring our training, equipment and experience—but we also come in friendship, to care for you and your growing family.

You never need to apologise for calling us, asking questions or telling us what you need. We are not coming to inspect your housekeeping. We are coming to support your birth.

So put the light on, move the Lego, give Pippin his own room—and leave the rest to us.

**Biscuits optional. Clear directions extremely welcome.**
